Dissertations, especially in computer science, can be very technical and
hard to explain to people who are not other computer scientists.
 However, I’m trying to explain my dissertation topic for people who do
not have any special training, and I thought a blog would be a good
place to do this because blogs are very informal.  I’m not sure how many
people will actually read this, but if it’s not entirely clear to you,
please write me a comment and let me know how I can improve it.  Also,
if you are technically inclined, feel free to comment as well.

The field of my dissertation is in natural language processing, which is
a subfield of computer science that aims to make computer programs that
can “process” human language. By “process” I mean that the computer
should be able to understand human language in some limited,
computational sense.  Some examples of natural language processing are:

- machine translation, e.g. <http://translate.google.com>
- speech recognition, e.g., Siri, on the latest greatest shiny ipad
- question answering, Siri would also be a good example of this
- dialog systems, Siri is another example, as are automated call centers
- text summarization, e.g. making an excerpt of a web page for display
  in search results
- dialog systems, e.g., chatbots, Siri, intelligent agents
- part of speech tagging, i.e., labeling words as nouns, verbs,
  prepositions, etc, which is used in many of the examples above.
- parsing, i.e. determining the syntactic structure of sentences, which
  is used in a lot of the above examples
- Natural language understanding or semantic analysis, which aims to
  determining the meaning of sentences
- affective computing and sentiment analysis, determining the emotional
  content of language
- text classification, which is classifying text into different
  categories, such as spam/not spam, world news/national news/sports
  news, etc., angry/happy/sad/neutral, author X/author Y/authorZ/…,
- topic modeling, trying to determine the topic of a document, which is
  like text classification but not knowing the set of topics beforehand
- …

Hopefully these examples provide an overview of natural language
processing, which is also known as NLP for short.  My dissertation topic
fits in a couple of these categories.  First of all, it is about
emotions, so it is in the affective computing subfield of NLP.  It is
also about the meaning of language about emotions, so it is also in the
natural language understanding or semantic analysis fields.  It also
deals with a dialog agent that asks questions, so it can be seen as
tangentially in the dialog system subfield.

Now that I’ve explained a bit about the general area of my dissertation
topic, let me say some more about how it is different and new.  In
affective computing and sentiment analysis, most previous work has
focused on determining the writer’s emotion or the emotion that the
writing will provoke in the reader.  I call this “expression of
emotions” in language.  My work focuses on description of emotions,
which are slightly different.  Description of emotion is when people
talk (or write) about emotions.  The reason why this is interesting and
important is that I can talk about sadness, despair, resentment,
jealousy, rage, vindication, pride, ecstasy, relief, and cheerfulness
without being or feeling any of these.  The previous sentence would have
seriously thrown off any algorithm that is trying to determine my
emotional state, or the emotion that is inspired in you, the reader.  So
I picked this area, with the help of my professors and labmates, which
we call *Natural Language Description of Emotion*, as a topic to study.
 Another reason why this area is interesting and important is that
animals are able to express their emotions, but humans are the only
species I know of that can describe and name emotions (that may or may
not be their own current emotions).  This is an important ability of
humans because it allows a great deal of introspection and allows us to
think about emotions hypothetically. On the downside, we humans aren’t
only feeling emotions “in the moment” like animals do, but imagining
about, gossiping about, and projecting emotions, and more.  Sometimes I
feel like writing a self-help book when I finish my dissertation!

So now having a topic,  that is somewhat interesting and important and
different from previous work, I needed a thesis statement.  Now that I
have given (hopefully) a gentle introduction, I need to unleash the
technical jargon.  It is not as complicated as it sounds, but I’m going
to write it now to inoculate the reader:

> Natural Language Descriptions of Emotion are Definite Descriptions
> that refer to Intersubjective Theoretical Entities.

See, that wasn’t that bad was it?  It sounds very technical but I can
explain it fairly easily if you, can patiently bear with me.  I’ve
already explained what natural language descriptions of emotion are.
 The next thing to explain is definite descriptions.  The notion of
definite descriptions was discovered by Bertrand Russell, a philosopher,
logician, and mathematician, among other things.  Definite descriptions
capture how people can talk about a specific, unique object.  If I see a
rabbit and point to it and say “rabbit”, you know that the meaning of
“rabbit” is the object that I’m pointing at.  However, we can talk about
objects that are not physically present and even though they are not
physically present, we can talk about them as if they were a unique
object.  The form of a description that refers to a unique object or
entity is what is known as a definite description.  An expression in the
form of “the” + noun, that is a noun preceded by the word “the”,  is a
definite description.  Proper names like “Abe Kazemzadeh” or “Bertrand
Russell” are also examples.

So why are we talking about “definite descriptions” again? First, I’m
claiming in the thesis statement that when we talk about and describe
emotions we are actually referring to something that is specifically and
uniquely describible.  We can claim that “happiness” is distinct from
“elation” based on how we describe them.  Also, we can claim that the
happiness I feel is the same as the happiness that you, the reader,
feels, even though we have a different personal histories and perhaps
some differences in our brain chemistry.  So this is the idea that I’m
trying to capture when I say that natural language descriptions of
emotion are definite descriptions.

The other reason why I introduce the idea of definite descriptions into
my dissertation is more technical, so I won’t go over that in too much
detail, but apart from the details it’s not that hard to understand.
 From a technical point of view, if we want to reduce statements in
human language to logic, we need to consider words as logical variables,
and in logic variables must refer to objects or sets of objects.
 However, in natural language we have words that refer to descriptions
rather than objects.  The technical aspect of definite descriptions
allows variables to stand for descriptions rather than objects or sets
of objects.  The whole business of reducing language to logic is
important because computers are essentially logic machines and to get
them to understand anything, you need to reduce it to logic.

This is a good point to introduce the last part of the thesis statement
“intersubjective theoretical objects”.  The idea of theoretical objects
was discovered by Rudolf Carnap, a philosopher of science.  He was
involved with trying to describe things logically, unambiguously, and in
a way that was empirically verifiable.  The way he proposed doing this,
was to only talk about things that are physically observable.  If you
try to do this, you’ll realize that is is very impractical, but it was a
provocative idea.  If you can only talk about physical objects, then
everything you say can be scientifically tested.  However, even
scientists talk about imaginary, unobservable things: for example, the
idea of an atom was essentially a such a fairy tale for more than two
thousand years, from the time that Democritus, the ancient Greek,
proposed it, to the time that it was physically studied in laboratories
in the late 1800’s and early 1900’s.  So actually, these unobservable
objects (at least before a certain point that they become observable),
are actually pretty important to science because they are like the
cutting-edge hypotheses that need to be tested.  These type of objects
that are not observable were called “theoretical objects (or entities)”
by Carnap.

In saying that natural language descriptions of emotion are definite
descriptions that refer to theoretical objects, what I mean is that we
may not (currently) be able to observe and test our language about
emotions, but at a certain point, we may be able to (for example if
there is some kind of brain physiology that gets discovered).
 Currently, we don’t know if happiness, anger, sadness, etc. are unique
physiological states, but we are able to talk about them as if they
were.

I actually think that some emotion descriptions will never be reduced to
an observable (e.g. physiological) basis, and that’s why I say that
natural language descriptions refer to *intersubjective* theoretical
entities. What I mean by this is that the experience of an emotion may
be subjective to a given person, but that the meaning of the words
describing the emotion are understood across subjects, i.e.
intersubjectively.  Furthermore, even if we could observe the subject’s
internal state, it wouldn’t matter for some emotion descriptions because
the meaning of the descriptions are determined by the conventional
meaning of language (i.e., being brought up in a linguistic community),
and  not determined by  some internal state.

To better illustrate intersubjectivity, compare the words “red”,
“rabbit”, and “bachelor” (I took these examples from a book called Word
And Object by Willard Van Orman Quine) .  “Red” refers directly to
sensory experience, so it is subjective, but we understand about how
eyes work so we know that there is some biological similarities in how
we experience “red”.  Also, the “edges” of the meaning of “red” are
gradual: if you slowly vary the shade/hue, you might slowly make
something into not red, but it will be gradual, not abrupt.  “Rabbit”
refers to a physical object, so it’s core meaning is not subjective,
although people might have different subjective associations about
rabbits, e.g., if they have had a pet.  “Bachelor” is unobservable and
subjective from a sensory point of view.  For a given person, they will
be able to determine who is a bachelor given their social relations.
 However, for a random person outside of their social relations, they
will not be able to say whether they are bachelors or not (for a female,
they will be able to say for sure that she is not, but for a random
male, they can only estimate, say given age, what is the likelihood of
being a bachelor).  However, if not restricted to sensory data, a person
can simply ask if an unknown male human is married or not.  The core
meaning of the word “bachelor” is not established by observation but
rather by language. This language-established-agreement-in-meaning is
what intersubjectivity is.   In saying that descriptions of emotion are
intersubjective, what I’m saying is that what we describe as an emotion
is as much determined by our language as it is by our physical
observations.  So of the three words, “red”, “rabbit”, and “bachelor”,
natural language descriptions of emotion are most similar to “bachelor”
in terms of the type of subjectivity they contain.

So now you should understand the thesis statement, the main claim of my
dissertation.  This part is the theoretical part.  There are two more
broad parts: the computational part, and the experimental part.  The
computational part involves making a model that specifies the details of
the thesis statement into a computer program.  The experimental part
involves testing the program in the wild, as it interacts with people.
 I’ll write about these other aspects of my dissertation shortly…
